issues.issue: "Fair and commercially reasonable terms" and "non-discriminatory basis" fix no rate, benchmark or method, so the content of the promise is open to opposing readings. It is also unclear whether "agrees to license" is a binding commitment or only an agreement to negotiate.

The 1994 statement's formulation differs from the later Motorola Letters of Assurance (e.g. the Option 2 commitment to "grant a license under reasonable rates"), raising a question which assurance governs the same 802.11 patents.

The reservation turns on whether "the standard may be followed without necessarily infringing such patents", an essentiality test whose boundary (mandatory vs optional portions, implementation choices) is not defined. That phrase decides which patents fall inside the licensing promise.
The carve-out limits the immediately preceding licensing assurance (c001) and the two could be read as reserving rights the assurance has already committed.

"Would upon request be willing to negotiate" a license on "reasonable terms and conditions including its then current royalty rates" is ambiguous between a binding licensing commitment and a mere agreement to negotiate, and "then current royalty rates" may or may not cap what is reasonable.

This willingness-to-negotiate language is weaker than the later Symbol Letters of Assurance's Option 2 ("The Patent Holder will grant a license under reasonable rates"), leaving it unclear which assurance controls Symbol's 802.11 patents.

The letter denies any grant of "copyrights or other intellectual property rights" while the preceding paragraph promises patent licensing, so the reach of the exclusion against the patent assurance could be argued.

"No license is implied by submission of this Letter of Assurance" can be read as negating any present obligation, which is in tension with the checked Option 2 commitment in the same form to grant licences on reasonable terms.

The parenthetical is garbled to the point of unintelligibility ("CA patent search is eae required"), so whether a patent search is required or not required cannot be read off the words. That word decides the disclosure duty.

"Is prepared to grant a license ... on reasonable terms and conditions" and "non-discriminatory basis" are undefined, and "prepared to grant" is ambiguous between a present binding promise and a statement of willingness. This is exactly the RAND language whose content the parties would dispute.
The commitment sits against the boxed statement in the same form that "No license is implied by submission of this Letter of Assurance", which can be read to deny the obligation the box creates.

The assurance runs "from the date of the standard's approval to the date of the standard's withdrawal", leaving unclear whether it binds before approval and whether licences taken during the period survive withdrawal.
